newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bonds retain bid bias, still needs data.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds retain bid bias, still needs data.

text.p: *Australian bonds retained Tuesday's bid bias with the 10-year bond futures contract testing a new 3-1/2 year high set in SYCOM at 93.270 shortly after the opening.
*Interest remains light ahead of Thursday's jobs data.
Australian bonds retained Tuesday's bid bias with the 10-year bond futures contract testing a new 3-1/2 year high set in SYCOM trading at 93.270 shortly after the opening.

This saw the yield on the benchmark October 2007 bond creep below 6.75 percent, while September bill futures also firmed and were just short of a contract high of 94.94, and all but discounting a 1/2 point cut in official 5.5 percent rates.
Traders said the firm tone was a hangover from Tuesday's rally on comments by Prime Minister John Howard that he wanted to see lower interest rates.
"It's all in futures at the moment, but I can't see the market pushing prices around too much ahead of Thursday's data, so it's likely to be another light day," one trader added.

Thursday's June labour force report is seen as one the key factors determining whether the Reserve Bank eases monetary policy, although there is a feeling that the bank is now hanging out for the inflation and wages data later this month before making a final decision.
Median expectations centre on an employment rise of 40,250, almost wiping out the 40,300 drop in May, but a much stronger figure is needed to show any real improvement in the sector.
The unemployment rate is seen dipping only a fraction to 8.7 percent from 8.8 percent, according to a Reuters survey of economists.

Meanwhile, the local market gleened little fresh impetus from action in U.S. Treasuries on Tuesday, finishing little changed with profit-taking after the recent strong rally being checked by buying on any dips.

The local market's firm tone saw it outperform the dollar bloc, pushing the Australian/U.S. 10-year spread back below 50 basis points. The short end of the New Zealand curve managed a small rally on a firmer bid N.Z. TWI, while Canadian debt saw a mild correction to its recent advance.
